messages.name: Marta Zlatic
messages.subject: Student mentorship inquiry: evidence for learning-guided action selection
messages.body:
Dear Dr Zlatic,

I'm Ethan Ramli, a 16-year-old Singaporean grade 11 student in Jakarta. I enjoy chess, and discovering the public adult fly connectome made me wonder whether a model using that wiring could learn to make better decisions through experience and feedback.

Your group's work on learning, action selection and circuit structure connects to the output side of my project. I understand that your larval fly work differs from the adult connectome I am using. I need to show that a learned signal causes a choice through an identified circuit path.

In all six simple tests, the model preferred the rewarded option more after training. But when I changed which option earned the reward, it chose the other option in only three tests. So it failed the full test. I haven't established whether the mechanism is biologically sound, and the chess part currently records feedback without learning from it.

I define the research question and training rubric, AI makes most of the code, and I am still learning the underlying methods. I have no research adviser. I'd like to develop this into a sound study that I could eventually submit to eLife.

Could you offer a pointer on this question: What minimum causal test would you require to show that a learned signal changes the selected action through an identified circuit? I'd appreciate your honest view of the approach. I can send a one-page methods summary first.

Thank you for your time,




Ethan Ramli




High-school student | Jakarta, Indonesia

messages.name: Misha Ahrens
messages.subject: Student mentorship inquiry: measuring flexible learning
messages.body:
Dear Dr Ahrens,

I'm Ethan Ramli, a 16-year-old Singaporean grade 11 student in Jakarta. I enjoy chess, and discovering the public adult fly connectome made me wonder whether a model using that wiring could learn to make better decisions through experience and feedback.

Your lab's work on whole-brain activity and behavioral flexibility connects to how I should measure learning. I understand that your zebrafish research is a different biological setting. My prototype sometimes keeps choosing the old rewarded option, so I need a measure that separates a changed neural response from a flexible choice.

In all six simple tests, the model preferred the rewarded option more after training. But when I changed which option earned the reward, it chose the other option in only three tests. So it failed the full test. I haven't established whether the mechanism is biologically sound, and the chess part currently records feedback without learning from it.

I define the research question and training rubric, AI makes most of the code, and I am still learning the underlying methods. I have no research adviser. I'd like to develop this into a sound study that I could eventually submit to eLife.

Could you offer a pointer on this question: Which behavioral measure or control would best expose a model that changes its response after feedback but does not adapt its choices? I'd appreciate your honest view of the approach. I can send a one-page methods summary first.

Thank you for your time,




Ethan Ramli
